title: LinkedIn
subtitle: 28 posting prompts based on 28 growth tactics, each with 3 ready-to-adapt examples for ADHD and Dopami.

profile.name: Abhishek K
profile.headline: Building Dopami (AI Agents for 380M+ ADHD minds)
facts: Co-founder, Dopami: building the AI cognitive layer for 380M+ people with ADHD (Sep 2025 – present)
Product Design Leadership, Flam: mixed-reality experiences reaching millions (2024–25)
National Institute of Design · India · 3,808 followers
Featured: “Flip the ADHD Switch” on YouTube

context: Context about me: I'm Abhishek K, co-founder of Dopami. We're building AI agents and an AI cognitive layer for the 380M+ people with ADHD; Done Together is our body-doubling and co-working space. Before Dopami I led product design at Flam (mixed-reality experiences reaching millions) and was Product Design Head at Betaflux. I studied at the National Institute of Design (NID). I have about 3,800 LinkedIn followers. My audience is adults with ADHD, ADHD coaches and clinicians, founders and product builders, and investors. Tone: honest, specific and human. No hype, no medical claims, no invented statistics. Use [placeholders] wherever a real number or story of mine is needed.
howToUse: Pick 3–5 prompts a week, from at least two different groups, so the feed mixes trust, craft and conversion.
Use “Copy prompt” to paste the prompt plus your profile context into Claude, then pick one of the 3 examples as the angle.
Fill every [placeholder] with a real number or story. If you don't have one yet, choose a different example.
Read the draft out loud (prompt 24) before posting, and log the result for your 30-day review (prompt 27).

categories.title: Cadence & mindset
categories.blurb: The habits that make everything else compound. Hard for an ADHD brain, which is exactly why they're worth posting about.

items.name: Post 3–5x/week
items.prompt: Write a short LinkedIn post that explains why posting 3–5 times a week beats posting once a week, using a simple before/after comparison of consistency vs intensity. Keep it under 150 words and end with a light CTA.
examples: Hyperfocus vs. habit: “My ADHD brain loves one 2,000-word Sunday post. My audience grew when I switched to four short ones.” Before/after: [your real numbers].
Tie it to the product: consistency over intensity is the same principle Dopami is built on. Fifteen minutes a day beats a heroic all-nighter, for tasks and for posting.
Build-in-public cadence: “4 posts a week while building Dopami = 4 small honest notes from the build, not 1 polished launch.” CTA: “What's your posting rhythm?”

items.name: Read posts out loud
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about the habit of reading every draft out loud before publishing. Share what kinds of problems this catches and why it improves engagement.
examples: ADHD honesty: “My drafts have three tangents per paragraph. Reading them out loud is how I find the one that matters.”
What it catches: run-on sentences, insider jargon (“cognitive layer” needs explaining out loud) and posts that never actually ask for anything.
The low-effort version: let your phone's text-to-speech read the draft back to you. Hearing it in someone else's voice exposes the clunky lines.

items.name: Review every 30 days
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about reviewing your content performance every 30 days. Include 3 specific metrics or questions to review and what to change based on the findings.
examples: Baseline post: “30 days ago I had 3,808 followers. Here's what changed, what I'm cutting and what I'm doubling down on.” Use your real end number.
Three questions: Which hooks earned profile visits? Which topics brought comments from ADHD coaches and builders? Which posts drove Dopami waitlist signups (via UTM)?
ADHD-friendly review: put it on a calendar, ask someone to sit with you while you do it (body doubling), and change one thing next month, not five.

items.name: Give it 90 days
items.prompt: Write a motivational yet practical LinkedIn post about committing to LinkedIn for 90 days. Use a growth-curve style narrative and end with the line “Give yourself 90 days.”
examples: The founder curve: “Weeks 1–4: crickets. Weeks 5–8: a few DMs from ADHD coaches. Weeks 9–12: the first people who found Dopami through a post.” Only include stages you actually hit.
The ADHD angle: “90 days is a long time for a brain that runs on novelty. Here's how I made it a streak instead of a resolution.”
From design leader to founder: “At Flam I shipped to millions. As a founder I started at zero. 90 days of posting is how I'm building that again.” End with “Give yourself 90 days.”

categories.title: Trust & topics
categories.blurb: What to talk about, and how to make people believe you. Your edge is lived ADHD reality plus years of product design craft.

items.name: Build know, like, trust
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that shows how to build know-like-trust through content. Use one personal example of a post that created trust, then give 3 specific content types that accelerate trust.
examples: The trust post: “The post that built the most trust wasn't a launch. It was admitting [a real ADHD moment, e.g. a deadline I set and missed].” Then: build-in-public updates, user stories (with consent), your own workarounds.
Show the work: “Years leading product design at Betaflux and Flam taught me trust comes from showing decisions, not polish. So I'm sharing Dopami's.”
Three post types that made people DM me about Dopami: a behind-the-scenes screen, a “what I got wrong” post and a plain-English body doubling explainer.

items.name: Pick better topics
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that shows how to choose better topics by combining audience pain + your unique experience. Include a quick “topic filter” checklist of 3–4 questions.
examples: Pain + experience: task paralysis (their pain) + designing first-time experiences for millions at Flam (your edge) = “What productivity apps get wrong in the first session for ADHD users.”
The filter: Does my audience feel this every week? Do I have a story only I can tell? Can I say it in one line? Does it lead toward Dopami without a pitch?
“Topics I killed this month”: show 3 generic AI-hype ideas that failed the filter, and the ADHD-specific one that replaced them.

items.name: Borrow from experts
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that smartly borrows an idea from an expert (with credit) and adds your own experience or twist. Show how to do this ethically and make it original.
examples: Credit Dr. Russell Barkley's line that ADHD isn't a problem of knowing what to do but of doing what you know. Then show how that one idea shapes how Dopami is designed.
Borrow BJ Fogg's “make it tiny” from Tiny Habits, then add your twist: for many ADHD brains, tiny isn't enough without a trigger or another person present.
Borrow a design principle you learned at NID and apply it to ADHD tools. Name the source, quote it exactly and spend most of the post on what you'd add.

items.name: Personal = IRL photo
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that pairs a personal story or insight with the instruction to use a real-life photo. Explain why authentic photos outperform stock images for building trust.
examples: Your actual desk mid-build (crop any screens with private info) plus a story from one real day of building Dopami.
The team in the room where you argue about onboarding (ask before posting anyone's face), plus one decision you made together this week.
An old NID sketchbook page, plus how design school shaped the way you now think about ADHD.

categories.title: Writing craft
categories.blurb: How the post is built: hooks, structure and length. Most of this applies to Dopami's product copy too.

items.name: Master curiosity gaps
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that opens with a strong curiosity gap, then delivers the payoff. Teach the reader how to create curiosity gaps without clickbait, using 2 clear examples.
examples: Hook: “The most productive hour of my week happens with my camera on and my mouth shut.” Payoff: body doubling, and why we built Done Together around it.
Clickbait vs. curiosity: “This ADHD hack changed my life” vs. “Why people with ADHD clean the whole kitchen instead of sending one email.”
Hook: “We cut the feature our early users asked for most.” Payoff: the reasoning. Only use this if it actually happened.

items.name: CPIO framework
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post explaining the CPIO framework (Convey → Package → Information) for writing better LinkedIn posts. Show one weak post vs one strong post rewritten with the framework.
examples: Weak: “Dopami helps people with ADHD focus using AI.” Strong: convey one idea (“Your tools assume a brain you don't have”), package it as a 3-line contrast, then give the information on how Dopami adapts.
Weak hiring post: “We're hiring a designer.” Strong: convey why the role matters, package it as “what you'd own in month one”, then give the information on how to apply.
Weak explainer: “Body doubling is a productivity technique.” Strong: convey the feeling, package it as a 25-minute story, then give the information on how to try it today.

items.name: Lead with outcome
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that leads with a clear outcome in the first line. Show the difference between a feature-led opener and an outcome-led opener with a before/after example.
examples: Feature-led: “Dopami uses AI agents that adapt to your brain.” Outcome-led: “Start the task you've been avoiding, today.” Keep the outcome honest; don't promise results you can't back up.
Hiring: “We're hiring a designer” vs. “Design the first product 380M ADHD minds don't have to fight.”
Video: “Watch our new video” vs. “If your focus disappears at 3pm, this video is for you.” Link the Flip the ADHD Switch video.

items.name: Complete tactical posts
items.prompt: Write a highly tactical LinkedIn post that someone can implement in under 10 minutes. Include numbered steps and zero fluff. Make the value immediate.
examples: Build a “launch pad” by your door in 10 minutes: one tray, then keys, wallet, phone and earphones, then a habit cue for the night before.
Your first body-doubling session today: pick a 25-minute block, invite one person on video, each say your task out loud, cameras on, start.
Make your phone less of a trap in 10 minutes: grayscale on, social apps off the home screen, notifications off for everything except people.

items.name: Keep posts concise
items.prompt: Write a concise LinkedIn post (under 120 words) that teaches one sharp idea. Demonstrate how cutting words increases clarity and engagement.
examples: “Your to-do list isn't a plan. It's a pile. Pick one thing. Make it smaller. Start.”
Show the edit: a 300-word Dopami update cut to 90 words, with both versions side by side.
One sharp idea: “Motivation usually follows starting, not the other way round.” Then say what that means for how Dopami is designed.

categories.title: Visual formats
categories.blurb: Match the format to the content: processes become infographics, lists become carousels, news gets a screenshot.

items.name: Processes = infographics
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that describes a process and explicitly recommends turning it into an infographic or carousel. Outline the exact steps that should appear in the visual.
examples: “How I turn a big task into a first step”: name the task → find the first verb → shrink it to 2 minutes → start a timer. Four panels.
“My weekly content system”: daily writing prompt → weekly reel ideas → B-roll shot list → one long video. A flow diagram.
“From user interview to shipped feature in 5 steps”, from your design-leadership years. One step per panel.

items.name: Listicles = Carousels
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post idea that works better as a carousel. Provide the hook + 5–7 slide titles so it can be turned into a carousel immediately.
examples: Hook: “7 signs your productivity system was built for a brain that isn't yours.” One sign per slide, with Dopami on the last slide.
Hook: “5 things I unlearned going from product design lead to founder.” One lesson per slide.
Hook: “6 ADHD myths, one per slide.” Myth in red, fact in plain type. Every fact must be supportable; link sources in the caption.

items.name: News = screenshots
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that comments on a piece of industry news and recommends using a screenshot. Show how to add original analysis so it's not just reposting.
examples: A new piece of ADHD research or a policy change: screenshot the headline, then add what it means for the people building tools, and what tools still can't fix.
A big AI model release: screenshot it, then explain what it changes (and what it doesn't) for assistive AI for neurodivergent users.
A mental-health tech funding round: screenshot it, then give your contrarian read on where the category is heading and where Dopami differs.

categories.title: Funnel & conversion
categories.blurb: Turn attention into waitlist signups, users, hires and investor conversations, without sounding salesy.

items.name: Make a content funnel
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that maps a simple content funnel (top → middle → bottom) for LinkedIn. Give one example post for each stage and explain what the reader should do next at every level.
examples: User funnel. Top: “Why your to-do list is why you never start” (follow). Middle: “How body doubling works and why we built Done Together” (visit profile). Bottom: “Opening [N] early-access spots” (comment or DM).
Hiring and fundraising funnel. Top: the 380M underserved vision. Middle: a build log showing progress. Bottom: “We're hiring a [role]” or “Raising our [round]”.
Video funnel. Top: a 30-second clip. Middle: the full Flip the ADHD Switch video. Bottom: the Dopami waitlist link.

items.name: Don't fear CTAs
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that demonstrates how to use clear CTAs without sounding salesy. Give 5 natural CTA examples that drive comments, DMs, or profile visits.
examples: Comment CTA: “If you've ever cleaned the whole kitchen instead of sending one email, tell me what your ‘kitchen’ is.”
Lead-magnet CTA: “Comment ‘START’ and I'll send you the 5-minute start ritual.”
DM CTA: “If you'd test Dopami for a week, DM me. I read every reply.” Profile CTA: “Follow along if you're building for neurodivergent users.”

items.name: Give away knowledge
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that gives away a useful piece of knowledge or framework for free. End by showing how giving knowledge away actually attracts the right clients.
examples: Give away your Seen / Helped / Belong content framework: make people feel seen, give them a small win, then invite them in.
Give away a body-doubling session template anyone can run with a friend on a video call.
Give away 3 ADHD-friendly design principles from your design work (for example, one decision per screen and visible progress), then explain why sharing them brings the right users and hires.

items.name: Track attribution (UTM)
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post explaining why tracking attribution with UTM links matters for content. Give a simple example of how to set it up and what decisions it helps you make.
examples: “Every link to Dopami's waitlist in my posts carries a UTM tag. Last month [X] signups came from [post type].” Use real numbers only.
Set it up: ?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=start-ritual. One campaign tag per post idea.
The decision it unlocked: which format to stop (for example, polished launch posts) and which to double down on (for example, raw ADHD moments).

items.name: Create free resources
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that promotes a free resource (checklist, template, or guide). Structure it so the post itself delivers value and the resource is a natural next step.
examples: “The 5-minute start ritual” checklist: put 3 of the steps in the post and the full version in the resource.
An ADHD-friendly weekly planning template (Notion or Google Sheets). Show one filled-in example in the post.
A body-doubling guide for remote teams. The post explains why it works; the guide covers how to run it every week.

categories.title: Distribution & outreach
categories.blurb: Posting is half the job. These cover finding, reaching and following up with the people Dopami is for.

items.name: Build a custom feed
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post teaching people how to build a high-signal custom feed. Include 3 specific steps and what to unfollow/mute so the algorithm works for you.
examples: Three steps: follow ADHD clinicians and researchers, follow neurodivergent founders and creators, and leave thoughtful comments on 10 of their posts a day.
“My feed used to be design portfolios. Now it's ADHD founders, coaches and parents. Here's how I rebuilt it in 20 minutes.”
What to mute: “wake up at 5am” hustle content. It's the opposite of what most ADHD brains need, and it trains your feed in the wrong direction.

items.name: DM 100 ICPs/week
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about the practice of DMing 100 ideal clients per week. Share a simple outreach structure that gets replies without being spammy, plus what to track.
examples: “I messaged 100 ADHD coaches in one week. Here's what I learned.” Share your real reply rate.
A three-line message: a specific line from their post, what you're building in one sentence, one question about their clients. No link in the first message.
What to track: messages sent → replies → calls → beta testers. Use a simple sheet, and say what you'd change in week two.

items.name: Mine sales calls
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that shows how to turn sales-call insights into content. Give 3 types of gold you can extract from calls and how to turn each into a post.
examples: Exact phrases from user interviews (“I'm not lazy, I'm stuck”) become hooks. Use them anonymously or with permission.
Objections become posts: an investor asked “Isn't this just a to-do app?” Here's my answer.
Aha moments become stories: “A beta user said [quote, with permission]. That one sentence changed our onboarding.”

items.name: Track ICP viewers
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about tracking who from your ICP is viewing your content. Explain a simple way to do this and how to follow up without being creepy.
examples: Weekly routine: check profile viewers and post analytics by job title (ADHD coaches, therapists, founders, investors). Note repeat visitors.
Follow-up: comment on their latest post first. If they keep engaging, send “Saw you've been following the Dopami build. What would make it useful for your clients?”
The no-creep rule: never open with “I saw you viewed my profile.” Lead with their work, not your analytics.

categories.title: Systems & learning
categories.blurb: Name what you do, learn from what didn't work, and use AI to do the research rather than the writing.

items.name: Name your processes
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that names a specific process you use (e.g. “The 3-Step Outreach Audit” or “The Weekly Content Sprint”). Break it down in 3–5 clear steps so readers can steal it.
examples: “The Body-Double Block”: one 25-minute session, one task said out loud, cameras on, a 2-minute check-in at the end.
“The 5-Minute Permission Rule”: start a task with permission to stop after five minutes, and notice how often you keep going.
“The Weekly Content Sprint”: Monday's reel ideas, a daily writing prompt and one batch-filming block. That's the system this website runs on.

items.name: Diagnose flops
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post that shows how to diagnose why a post flopped. Give 3 common reasons posts underperform and the exact fix for each, based on real patterns.
examples: “My post about Dopami's AI architecture flopped. Diagnosis: a feature-led hook, no person in it, and no clear ask.” Fix: lead with a user's moment.
Three reasons: the hook was about us rather than them, it was too long to read on a phone, and it never said what to do next. Give the fix for each.
Statistics vs. stories: compare a numbers-led ADHD post with a lived-moment post using your real data. Only draw the conclusion if your data supports it.

items.name: Use AI for research
items.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about using AI for research (not writing). Show a practical workflow: how to feed AI the right inputs, extract insights, and turn them into original posts without sounding robotic.
examples: Paste 20 anonymized user-interview notes into Claude, ask for the phrases people repeat, and turn the most repeated one into a hook written in your own words.
Use AI to collect the questions people ask about ADHD and focus in public forums, then answer the best one from your own experience.
Give AI your last 30 posts and their stats, and ask what separates the top 5 from the bottom 5. You write the post; the AI finds the pattern. An AI-for-ADHD founder doing this is on-brand.
